This page covers the exact U.S. O*NET/SOC occupation 47-3014.00, Helpers--Painters, Paperhangers, Plasterers, and Stucco Masons: helping painters, paperhangers, plasterers, or stucco masons through duties requiring less skill, including using, supplying, or delivering materials and tools and cleaning work areas and equipment. Official scope: Help painters, paperhangers, plasterers, or stucco masons by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. O*NET lists core tasks including the following (the page lists 11 tasks and displays the first 5 by default): cleaning work areas and equipment; supplying or holding tools and materials; applying protective coverings, such as masking tape, to objects or areas that could be damaged or stained by work processes; smoothing surfaces of objects to be painted using sanding and buffing tools and equipment; and erecting scaffolding. Common job titles include Helper, Painter Helper, Painter Assistant, Plaster Helper, and Plaster Tender. Coverage note: the U.S. wage and employment data presented on O*NET's 47-3014.00 page are not marked as coming from a broader or neighboring occupation, so this page identifies them as data for this occupation itself (47-3014.00). In the U.S., it is in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0). This page does not extrapolate U.S. classifications to job titles, qualifications, or wages in mainland China.

Practice brief | A wholly fictional painting and plastering assistance task package (for practicing the process only; it does not represent any real company, project, or data). Draft a plan explaining: (1) how to use a fictional work order and materials list to assist systematically with surface preparation and painting or plastering, covering the work location and drawing number, substrate material and condition, specifications for paint or mortar, putty, and masking materials, mixing and stirring, surface preparation, sanding and dust removal, masking and protection, scaffolding, work at height and ventilation, and cleaning, curing and protection after work; identify missing information that needs to be supplied, including substrate moisture content and existing coatings, site conditions and ventilation and fire prevention requirements, safety, access and work permit requirements, material deliveries and sequencing; (2) how to design completion and review points for a fictional materials and work record, covering fields and definitions, location and batch identifiers, materials, mix ratios and quantities, surface preparation and masking, painting or plastering and curing, abnormalities, rework and outstanding items, and original records and revision trails; (3) how to write a shift and work summary suitable for handover, covering location—materials and mix ratios—surface preparation—painting or plastering—cleaning and curing—outstanding items and recommendations; (4) how to record and retain materials and work data and distinguish public information from controlled project and supplier information; and (5) how to pause, review, isolate and report when solvent, paint, chemical, height or dust hazards, actions beyond job authorization, or safety risks are identified. Answer using public sources and simulated data, without any real company or project data.

Fit signals | Work activity importance ratings for U.S. O*NET 47-3014.00 show that inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (80), getting information (79), performing general physical activities (78), controlling machines and processes (77), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (76), and identifying objects, actions, and events (76) are the occupation's most important activities. Work context indicates frequent face-to-face discussions (84% daily), close collaboration with painters, plasterers and coworkers (73% in constant contact with others), prolonged standing (68% continually or almost continually), relatively frequent decisions (48% daily), common exposure to contaminants (37% daily), and constraints from project schedules and work sequencing. If you are willing to provide hands-on assistance with surfaces, materials and tools, can thoroughly carry out surface preparation, masking, sanding, and painting or plastering according to skilled workers' instructions and procedures, and take responsibility for work safety, process quality and site order, the occupation's daily demands may be closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also reports, for 47-3014.00 work context and tasks, common exposure to contaminants (37% daily), prolonged standing (68% continually or almost continually), frequent work in cramped spaces or at height and on scaffolding, consequences of error most often rated fairly serious (35% fairly serious, 22% serious, 16% very serious), substantial responsibility for others' health and safety (37% high responsibility, 22% very high responsibility), and time pressure from sequencing and schedules (34% daily). This occupation works with paint, solvents, mortar, putty, substrates and scaffolding. A single instance of improper solvent, paint or chemical handling, inadequate surface preparation or masking, inadequate scaffolding or fall protection, or a sanding or spraying error may cause surface rework, material waste, injury, schedule delays and compliance risks. O*NET places it in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0). Its education section reports that 68% indicate less than a high school diploma is required, 26% a high school diploma or equivalent, and 4% a postsecondary certificate (the three categories listed on that page). Growth is labeled Slower than average (2%), and the page does not display Bright Outlook. If working around dust, contaminants, noise, solvent odors, heights and cramped spaces is difficult for you, or you struggle with a pace that varies by project, sequencing and weather and may involve overtime, or are unwilling to take responsibility for safety and coordinated work, treat these as practical costs.

Responsibility judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can do three things within the same assignment: deliver sound technical work by completing mixing, surface preparation, sanding, masking, painting or plastering, cleaning and curing according to procedures and skilled workers' instructions, producing usable materials and work records; manage safety, compliance and boundaries by working and keeping records in line with solvent, paint, chemical, ventilation, fire prevention, scaffolding, height, open-edge and dust requirements, distinguishing public information from controlled project and supplier information and handling it under established procedures, and avoiding unauthorized scaffold erection or dismantling, mixing or other actions beyond your remit; and accept defined job responsibilities by taking responsibility for your own mixing, surface preparation, masking, painting or plastering, cleaning and records, while referring matters beyond your authorization or involving specialized work or major safety issues to the appropriate roles or organizations under established procedures. Test this through a verifiable experience, such as producing an assistance plan and an explanation of materials and work records for a fictional work order, or reviewing the handling of a solvent, height or sanding abnormality, rather than relying only on an interest questionnaire.

Direct answer | This page's Helpers--Painters, Paperhangers, Plasterers, and Stucco Masons is the exact O*NET occupation 47-3014.00. Its work falls into several categories: (I) materials and preparation—supplying or holding tools and materials, organizing and storing materials, tools and equipment, delivering mortar to plasterers and helping mix it; (II) surface preparation—smoothing surfaces of objects to be painted with sanding and buffing tools and equipment, and filling cracks or damaged areas in plaster with putty or epoxy materials; (III) masking and protection—applying protective coverings, such as masking tape, to objects or areas that could be damaged or stained by work processes; (IV) application assistance—helping painters, paperhangers, plasterers and stucco masons prepare surfaces and carry out their work; and (V) cleaning and closeout—cleaning work areas and equipment, helping remove leftover materials and protective layers, and restoring the site.

The exact occupation 47-3014 assists painters, paperhangers, plasterers or stucco masons with less-skilled tasks, delivering tools and materials and cleaning. Its current 11 tasks comprise 7 Core and 4 Supplemental tasks. Cleaning 82, supplying 79, masking 72, sanding 69, erecting scaffolding 61, assisting 55, and filling cracks 55 are Core; mixing plaster 41 and paint-stripping tank tasks 33 / 33 / 31 are Supplemental and are not shared duties of every position. The original activity ratings—inspection 80, information 79, physical activity 78, control 77 and communication 76—are correctly retained. For the exact U.S. BLS occupation 47-3014, typical entry requirements are no formal educational credential, no related work experience, and short-term on-the-job training. O*NET's new-hire figures of 68% below high school, 26% high school and 4% postsecondary certificate are surveyed requirements, not Chinese entry requirements or the educational composition of all workers. RC interests are for exploration only. Current work style scores of dependability 66, cooperation 52, attention to detail 46 and cautiousness 41 describe the occupation and do not predict individual performance.

Responsibility introduction | Efficiency can be delegated to equipment and systems; on-site mixing, surface preparation, sanding and masking judgments, safety and process responsibility cannot. The following five steps identify human responsibilities that must be preserved before and after adopting digital tools or automated data and report generation.

Tasks and boundaries: skilled workers and personnel with relevant experience and authorization must define location, material, chemical and safety boundaries. Equipment and systems do not replace site and process judgments.

Data and methods: you must check and review quantities, mix ratios, materials, progress data, sources and validation. Explicitly state data gaps or deviations; do not conceal gaps with system outputs.

Conclusions and determinations: you must draw conclusions about mixing, surface preparation, masking, application and cleaning according to procedures and current acceptance standards. System outputs must not directly authorize release, rework or external publication.

Safety and compliance: solvents, paint, chemicals, ventilation, fire prevention, scaffolding, heights, open edges, dust, work permits and personal protection must comply with construction safety and occupational health requirements and established procedures. Manage controlled information according to confidentiality and retention requirements.

Changes and disclosure: disclosure of materials, mix ratios and process information, and formulation or design changes, must remain within authorization and established procedures. Pause, isolate and report solvent, height, sanding or authorization-related abnormalities according to procedures.

subject.summary: This page covers the exact O*NET/SOC occupation 47-3014.00, Helpers--Painters, Paperhangers, Plasterers, and Stucco Masons: helping painters, paperhangers, plasterers, or stucco masons by performing duties requiring less skill, including using, supplying, or delivering materials and tools and cleaning work areas and equipment. Core tasks include cleaning work areas and equipment; supplying or holding tools and materials; applying protective coverings, such as masking tape, to objects or areas that could be damaged or stained by work processes; smoothing surfaces of objects to be painted using sanding and buffing tools and equipment; and erecting scaffolding. Common job titles include Helper, Painter Helper, Painter Assistant, Plaster Helper, and Plaster Tender. Official scope: Help painters, paperhangers, plasterers, or stucco masons by performing duties requiring less skill. Duties include using, supplying, or holding materials or tools, and cleaning work area and equipment. Coverage note: the U.S. wage, employment, and industry data presented on O*NET's 47-3014.00 page are not marked as coming from a broader or neighboring occupation, so this page identifies them as data for this occupation itself (47-3014.00). The occupation is in Job Zone 1-2 (little or no preparation to some preparation needed), below 6.0 (SVP Below 6.0). Growth for 2024—2034 is Slower than average (2%).
